I’m a nurse in the ER, and a 13 year-old came in tonight bleeding and doubled over in pain.

She was losing her pregnancy.

Her mother and father arrived while the doctor was still explaining it to her.

Her mother looked at her and said, “Well, maybe this is for the best.”

Her father shook his head and said, “Do you know what people would have said?”

That was it. That was what they said to their daughter.

Neither of them asked if she was in pain. Neither of them asked if she was okay. Neither of them reached for her hand.

She was lying there shaking, and they were standing at the foot of the bed worrying about what the neighbors would think.

And then she whispered, so quietly I almost missed it, “I wanted this baby.”

I just need to sit with that for a second, because I am struggling.

She is somebody’s daughter. She came in scared, bleeding, and grieving something she hadn’t even gotten to say out loud yet, and the two people who were supposed to hold her up looked at her like she was an inconvenience.

The doctor didn’t say a word at first. She just walked over, put herself between the bed and the parents, and said, “I need you both to leave this room. Right now.”

They left.

I wanted to stand up and applaud in the middle of a hospital room. I didn’t. I just stood there with a blanket in my hands, trying very hard not to cry in front of a patient.

The doctor pulled a chair up to the bed, took the girl’s hand, and said, “I’m so sorry. You’re allowed to be sad. Take all the time you need.”

She cried so hard the whole bed shook. I tucked the blanket around her and stayed until her breathing slowed down.

I don’t have a lesson for this one. I don’t have anything wrapped up neatly.

I walked out to the parking lot after my shift and sat in my car for twenty minutes without turning it on.

When I finally called my husband, I couldn’t get a single word out, and he just stayed on the line with me.

I hope she knows that her pain mattered to somebody in that building tonight.

I hope she knows she was not alone.

I have followed recent reports of violence accompanying political events in different parts of the country. 

Every form of violence stands condemned. Violence should never have a place in our political campaigns as we move toward the 2027 general elections. 

Our campaigns should be about issues, a contestation of ideas that promote the welfare of our people and the progress of our country. 

As the leader of this country, I commit myself to a peaceful, free, and fair election, and I urge political leaders and supporters across party lines to conduct themselves responsibly. 

I have said that being in different political parties or pursuing different ambitions does not make us enemies. 

As Nigerians, we are members of the same household living in different rooms. Therefore, our politics must elevate human conditions and focus on national progress and development. 

I want to reiterate my previous directive to the security agencies: be strict and firm against anyone who seeks to test our resolve and will to preserve public order. 

Our administration is committed to an orderly and peaceful election, and all political parties and candidates should be protected and free to campaign anywhere in the country without molestation or fear for their safety. 

We shall not tolerate any irresponsible conduct by politicians and their supporters. 

Security agencies are therefore authorised to confront thuggery and other anti-social and anti-democratic activities with full force.

Bola Ahmed Tinubu 
President and Commander-in-Chief, Federal Republic of Nigeria
